docs.title: Gradus
docs.text:
An unofficial installer for GNU Guix System. The installer runs from a console wizard or an answer file, and its output is a config.scm — the machine is installed from that file and the file is kept on the machine afterwards.

Document Type What it is Architecture explanation layers, data contracts, filesystem capability table, invariants Contract reference invocation modes, answer schema, artefacts, exit status Pages reference the wizard surface, page by page Install flow explanation the install pipeline, stage by stage Implementation explanation language, module layout, upstream boundary Testing how-to acceptance tests T1–T10 and the install matrix Upstream explanation what is offered to Guix and how

Repository: Zhen-LinHuo/gradus.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Gradus is one installer with many frontends. The core — the answer schema, the wizard state machine, the storage operations and the install pipeline — knows nothing about terminals, browsers or screens. A frontend renders the core's data and feeds it input. The console TUI (gradus/script.scm --tui) is the first frontend; a web frontend is planned and must reuse the same core without changes to it.

Contract version: 1. Product version: 0.3.0.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph core["core — pure data and pure functions, no UI imports"]
        ANS["answers.scm<br/>answer schema and validation<br/>(raises typed conditions)"]
        WIZ["wizard.scm<br/>page and field state machine<br/>(fields are plain data)"]
        SEL["selection models<br/>(channels, substitutes, proxy,<br/>package patterns, kernel arguments)"]
        FS["filesystem capability table<br/>(one row per supported file system)"]
        OPS["storage.scm · install.scm<br/>render.scm · serialize.scm"]
    end
    subgraph fe["frontends — thin clients"]
        TUI["tui.scm<br/>(ncurses)"]
        WEB["web frontend (planned)"]
        CLI["--config / --answers<br/>(no interaction)"]
    end
    TUI --> WIZ
    WEB --> WIZ
    WIZ --> ANS
    WIZ --> SEL
    WIZ --> OPS
    OPS --> FS

The rule that keeps the layers honest: core modules must not import a frontend, and a frontend must not reach past the wizard state machine into storage or install code. Anything a frontend needs from the core must be expressible as part of the data contracts below.

docs.title: The data contracts of the core
1. The answer schema (answers.scm)
docs.text: The single source of truth for what an installation decision is. Keys, types, required fields and cross-field rules live here. Both frontends and the CLI validate against it; the validator is the same code.

docs.title: 2. The wizard page model (wizard.scm)
docs.text:
A page is a list of fields; a field is plain data:

(label, kind, value, options)

kind is one of menu, text, password, check, action. Defaults, option lists and per-field validation are data, not code paths in a frontend. The TUI draws this structure with ncurses; a web frontend renders the same structure as HTML. When a page needs a new widget, the field kind is added here first, and every frontend implements it.

docs.title: 3. Selection models
docs.text:
Everything the operator selects rather than types is a core data model, never a frontend feature:

model shape notes channels ordered list of (name, url, commit) order is authority order; the official channel is always available and never hidden substitutes ordered list of (url, kind, key) order is preference order — the first reachable server wins; adding a server places it first proxy (http, https, no_proxy) applied to the live daemon for the install and persisted to the target package patterns curated groups, see below the fast path for a sensible base system kernel arguments preset + free list offered as keep-default / none / edit

Package patterns follow the idea the openSUSE installer calls patterns: a named group of packages that yields a working set of functionality — "remote access", "monitoring tools", "network utilities" — instead of asking the operator to know package names. Each pattern is a core data row:

(pattern (name 'remote-access)
         (description "SSH and terminal multiplexing")
         (packages (list "openssh" "tmux" "rsync")))

The installed set is %base-packages + the chosen profile + the selected patterns + explicitly named packages, expanded by render.scm into one manifest. Patterns are curated in this repository and versioned with it; resolving them dynamically against a channel is a possible later extension. Per-user software after installation is the domain of guix home and out of scope here.

All five models are consumed by install.scm uniformly: changing the substitute list or the proxy restarts the live guix-daemon with the new settings as a fixed step of the install pipeline, not a special case.

docs.title: 4. The filesystem capability table
docs.text:
A supported file system is one row of data, not a set of branches scattered across modules. The general handling is uniform: prepare creates the file system with its label, identification reads the label and UUID back, the mount step addresses the volume by that identification, render.scm and serialize.scm declare it, and the boot row states what the bootloader needs to know.

question answered by which package provides the tools tool-package how to create it and set its label mkfs tool and label flag how to read back its label and UUID identify command how the mounted source is addressed mount-source: label, UUID or device what the Guix declaration looks like declaration what the bootloader needs to know boot-notes

Adding a file system is adding a row and running the acceptance matrix in docs/testing.md; no module gains a new special case.

Known exception — identification on btrfs. libblkid could not read a btrfs file system created by current btrfs-progs, whose default on-disk format (block-group-tree) predates libblkid's parser. The btrfs row therefore identifies with btrfs filesystem show, which reads the superblock natively. Every other row identifies with blkid -o export. Prepare, mount and declaration code consume the row's identify command and never invoke blkid directly.

docs.title: 5. Typed conditions
docs.text:
The core raises structured conditions, never prints. A condition carries a category and a message:

category meaning decision the operator's input is incomplete or contradictory environment the machine or the network refuses — a busy or missing disk, a missing tool, an unreachable server defect the installer itself failed

Frontends render conditions in their own idiom — the TUI below the form that caused them, a web frontend as structured JSON. Categories are not exit codes: the mapping onto docs/contract.md §7 follows the contract, not the category. decision exits 2; an environment refusal before anything is written to the target exits 3, one encountered during installation exits 4; a defect exits 4. The CLI entry point applies the mapping, so every frontend inherits it.

docs.title: Implementation status
docs.text: Implemented today: the answer schema and validator, the wizard page model with its back semantics, typed conditions, the storage operations for the supported file systems, and the TUI. In the tree but data-driven only partially: substitutes, proxy and kernel arguments follow the selection models; the package-pattern table and the filesystem capability table are specified here and land with the refactor that consumes them. The web frontend is planned. Until a section is implemented, docs/contract.md section 2 and docs/pages.md remain the authority on what the software accepts today.

docs.title: Cross-cutting invariants
docs.text:
Secrets. Passphrases and passwords never appear in a command line, a log line or the provenance record. The only transport is with-secret-file: a 0600 file on /dev/shm, passed to the tool by path and removed when the operation ends.

Logs. The core writes /var/log/gradus-install.log with stage markers ([1/4] … [4/4]). Frontends display log output; they never write it.

Language. User-visible strings are tables in the core. The console TUI serves English only — the Linux console cannot render CJK with its fixed 512-glyph font — and the web frontend serves the same tables including Chinese. Translating is filling one table, not touching two codebases.

docs.title: Frontend requirements
docs.text:
A Gradus frontend is a thin client that:

  1. renders the wizard page model (fields, options, defaults) and the selection models (lists, orderings, checkboxes);
  2. captures input and applies the back semantics uniformly — inside an edited field, back cancels the edit; on a page, back moves one page earlier; the state machine decides how far back "back" goes;
  3. renders typed conditions verbatim, including the category;
  4. never formats or second-guesses core data. If the frontend needs a string the core does not provide, the core grows it.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: The product is developed as a source checkout and ships as a Guix package: guix.scm defines it, so the installer can be built with guix build -f guix.scm, referenced by other Guix packages, and — as a channel — consumed directly by image build pipelines that want to embed the installer in a medium. A live medium is one such artefact: a downstream image recipe that boots into the wizard with the required tools present. The core carries no knowledge of any medium.

docs.title: Testing layers
docs.text:
layer what it proves where unit validators, layout arithmetic, serialization, page model transitions make check walkthrough a frontend accepts a scripted input sequence across all pages scripted pty / driver install matrix one VM install per file-system row × firmware docs/testing.md T2/T9/T10

A change that passes the unit layer but not the install matrix is not done; the filesystem findings that produced the capability table were all matrix-layer discoveries.

docs.title: The installer contract
docs.text:
This document is the authoritative definition of what the installer accepts, what it produces, and what it promises. Anything that consumes the installer — a fleet repository, a CI job, a human with a USB stick — may rely on this file and on nothing else.

Contract version: 1. Product version: 0.3.0.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
The installer turns installation decisions into an installed Guix System and into the operating-system declaration that describes it.

It is not a configuration manager. After installation, the machine is managed with guix system reconfigure and the configuration file the installer left behind.

docs.title: 2. Invocation modes
docs.text:
Implementation status (v0.2). Of this section, the following exist today: --config FILE and --answers FILE, --root DIR (the mount point under which the target's file systems are mounted; default /mnt), --dry-run, --log, --version. In --config mode the target's file systems must already exist, carrying the labels or UUIDs that FILE names — the installer mounts them and does not partition. In --answers mode the target disk is prepared from the answer file. --target, --erase, --proxy, --no-proxy and --yes are specified but not implemented yet.

Mode Command shape What is required What is written Interactive gradus Nothing Target disk, only after explicit confirmation From configuration gradus --config FILE --target DEV FILE's file systems must resolve on the target Target disk, bootloader Unattended gradus --answers FILE --target DEV --erase Complete answer file Everything the answers describe Validation any of the above plus --dry-run As above Nothing

--dry-run performs every check, renders the resulting operating-system, prints it to standard output, and exits without touching any device.

docs.title: 2.1 Option reference (v1)
docs.text:
Option Effect --config FILE Install this operating-system declaration as written --answers FILE Read installation decisions from FILE; render the configuration from them --target DEV Device that receives the bootloader (and, with --erase, the system) --erase Permit writing to DEV. Without it, a device carrying a file system is refused --proxy URL Use this HTTP/HTTPS proxy for the installation, overriding the answer file --no-proxy LIST Comma-separated hosts that bypass the proxy, overriding the answer file --dry-run Check and print; write nothing --yes Answer confirmation prompts affirmatively (requires --erase for destructive modes) --log FILE Write the transcript to FILE in addition to the default location --version Print product and contract version, exit 0

--config and --answers are mutually exclusive. --target is mandatory in both non-interactive modes.

docs.title: 3. Configuration mode
docs.text:
In --config mode the installer does not modify the declaration. It:

  1. validates the declaration (guix system build --dry-run equivalent);
  2. checks that every file-system device in it resolves on the target — by label or UUID, before any mount is attempted;
  3. checks that the bootloader target is plausible (UEFI system partition present, or BIOS boot area available);
  4. mounts the declared file systems under the target root;
  5. runs guix system init with the declaration;
  6. installs the bootloader as the declaration describes.

Device names in the declaration are therefore a caller concern. This mode deliberately performs no partitioning: a configuration cannot express partition sizes, so inferring a layout from it would be guesswork.

docs.title: 4. Answer-file format
docs.text:
An answer file is an S-expression read with Scheme's read. It describes the installation, not the whole system: it carries facts and a small number of policies, and the renderer fills in everything else from the selected profile.

;; answers.scm — schema version 1
((schema-version . 1)
 (profile . "desktop")
 (locale . "en_GB.utf8")
 (timezone . "Europe/London")
 (keyboard . "gb")
 (host-name . "workstation")

 (proxy
  (http . "http://proxy.example.net:3128")
  (https . "http://proxy.example.net:3128")
  (no-proxy . ("localhost" "cache.example.net")))

 (source
  (channels . "channels.scm")
  (substitute-services
   ((name . "official")
    (url . "https://ci.guix.gnu.org")
    (kind . official))
   ((name . "lan-cache")
    (url . "http://cache.example.net")
    (kind . builder)
    (key . "cache.example.net.pub"))))

 (storage
  (mode . simple)                 ; simple | lvm | existing
  (disk . "/dev/nvme0n1")
  (erase . #f)
  (esp-size . 1024)               ; MiB; the ESP (EFI) or BIOS Boot partition
  (swap-size . 0)                 ; MiB; 0 means no swap partition
  (root-size . 0)                 ; MiB; 0 means the rest of the disk
  (encryption (mode . luks)       ; LUKS1 — GRUB must read the root at boot
              (name . "cryptroot")
              (passphrase . "…")) ; never written to the declaration
  (data-volumes . ()))            ; never formatted unless erase? is #t per volume

 (boot
  (bootloader . grub-efi)         ; grub-efi | grub-bios | extlinux | u-boot | none
  (target . "/dev/nvme0n1")
  (kernel . linux-libre)
  (extra-kernel-arguments . ("console=ttyS0,115200"))
  (timeout . 5)                   ; -1 waits indefinitely
  (stop-at-menu . #f)
  (default-entry . 0)
  (update-nvram . #t)
  (keep-generations . 5))

 (network
  (management . dhcp)             ; dhcp | static
  (interface . "eno1"))

 (users
  ((name . "alice")
   (groups . ("wheel" "audio" "video"))
   (ssh-keys . ("ssh-ed25519 AAAA..."))))

 (software
  (extra-packages . ())
  (manifest . #f)))

Rules:

  • Unknown keys are an error, not ignored. Silent acceptance of a typo is how an unattended install ends up different from what the operator reviewed.
  • Every key in the example above is optional except schema-version, profile, storage and users; omitted keys take documented defaults.
  • erase defaults to #f. A data volume is never formatted implicitly; each volume carries its own erase? flag.
  • bootloader may be none. In that case no bootloader is installed and the existing one is left untouched; the renderer omits the field and the review stage states plainly that the machine will not boot unaided.
  • A substitute service's kind decides whether a key is required. mirror serves official store paths signed by their original builders and needs no new key; builder signs its own artefacts and must carry one.
  • Proxy credentials are secrets. They are never printed in full, and they are written to the target only when the operator asks for that.
  • Command-line --proxy and --no-proxy override the corresponding answer-file values; the answer file is not rewritten to match.
  • The renderer is deterministic: the same answer file and the same profile at the same version produce the same declaration.
  • Encryption is refused where the installer cannot honour it, before anything is written to a disk: with lvm storage, and together with a swap partition (the swap would be plaintext outside the container). The passphrase is used to format the container and is never written to the declaration; the declaration carries the container's LUKS UUID, which is the only form GRUB can unlock. A declaration without that UUID is not written.

docs.title: 4.1 Sources and trust
docs.text:
The installer never adds a source of its own. The source list in the answer file is used in the order written, both in the live environment and in the target's guix-configuration.

Signature checking is never relaxed. A mirror accelerates; it does not vouch. The keys authorised for the live environment are the same keys written into the target, so a key that is only present during installation does not silently disappear at the first boot.

docs.title: 5. Artefacts
docs.text:
On the target, after a successful installation:

Path Content /etc/config.scm The exact operating-system declaration that was installed /etc/gradus/answers.scm The answers used, or a statement that --config mode was used /etc/gradus/provenance.scm Installer version, contract version, Guix revision, UTC timestamp /var/log/gradus-install.log Full transcript

/etc/config.scm is byte-identical to the file that was reviewed: no reformatting, no regeneration after the fact. Provenance exists so that "what is on this machine" and "what was requested" can be compared without guesswork.

docs.title: 6. Guarantees
docs.text:
1. No implicit destruction. A device is written only when it is named by --target and erasure is requested (--erase in unattended mode, an explicit confirmation in interactive mode).
  2. No hidden sources. Packages are fetched only from the channels and substitute URLs declared in the answers or configuration. The installer does not add sources of its own.
  3. Dry run is inert. --dry-run creates no mount, no partition, no file.
  4. Refusal over guessing. If a declared file system does not resolve, if the bootloader target is ambiguous, or if the target is mounted or is the live medium, the installer stops with a non-zero exit status. It does not pick a default device.
  5. Provenance. A successful installation always leaves the artefacts in §5.
  6. Proxy where it is needed. A proxy configured for the installation is used for every fetch the installation performs, and is configured for the target's Guix daemon. A no_proxy entry always takes precedence, so a local cache is not sent through the proxy that provides external access.

docs.title: 7. Exit status
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Usage error 2 Validation error in the configuration or answer file 3 Target unsuitable (mounted, missing, too small, live medium, insufficient privileges) 4 Installation failed 5 Interrupted by the operator

After exit 3 or 4, the installer reports exactly which step failed and what is currently on the target. It does not attempt an automatic repair.

docs.title: 8. Non-guarantees
docs.text:
• No resume of a partially written disk in v1. A failed installation is re-attempted from the beginning; the operator is told what state the target is in.
  • No migration or upgrade of an installed system.
  • No post-install configuration. That is guix system reconfigure's job.
  • No rollback of an activation performed on a running live system. The installer installs; it does not mutate a running system.

docs.title: 9. Compatibility and versioning
docs.text:
• Contract version changes only when an existing caller would break: option removal, answer-file key removal, artefact path change, altered guarantee. Product major version follows the contract major version.
  • Product version is SemVer. Adding a page, an optional answer key or a target architecture is a minor bump.
  • The answer file declares its own schema-version; the installer refuses a schema it does not implement rather than ignoring unknown fields.
  • Supported Guix System: the current stable release at the time of the product release, recorded in /etc/gradus/provenance.scm.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Product version: 0.3.0. Contract version: 1.

docs.title: Language: Guile Scheme
docs.text:
The installer is written in Guile Scheme, the language of Guix itself.

The decision is not sentimental. Three properties follow from it:

  1. One configuration model. The artefact is a Scheme program. Generating it in the same language that evaluates it means there is no second, approximate model of operating-system, services or gexps to keep in step.
  2. Errors come from the same evaluator. A malformed declaration fails in the same place, with the same message, whether it was written by hand or rendered from answers.
  3. The upstream path stays open. Guix's own installer lives in gnu/installer/. A Scheme implementation can contribute pages there as patches; an implementation in another language can only contribute ideas.

Two practical consequences reinforce the choice: the installation image already contains Guile and Guix, so there is no extra runtime closure to ship, and the project can be packaged as an ordinary Guix package.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Language Attraction Why not (for now) Rust Static binary, strong TUI and testing ecosystem; a working third-party Guix installer already exists in Rust The configuration model would be rebuilt in a second language or reduced to text templates, and nothing could be offered upstream Python Fastest to write Adds a runtime and a dependency surface to the image, and still rebuilds the model Go Single binary, simple deployment Same model problem as Rust, with a smaller Guix-adjacent community

A non-Scheme implementation is not impossible; it is a different product strategy. This repository has chosen the one described above.

docs.title: Boundary with Guix
docs.text:
Use Guix's modules to construct and inspect declarations. Use the guix command as a subprocess to build, validate and install.

The reason for the split is ABI discipline. Guix's internal modules change between releases; the command-line interface is a documented contract. Anything that must match the installed Guix exactly — resolving derivations, building the system, running guix system init — goes through the command line. Record construction and answer validation use the modules, where a version mismatch is a build error rather than a silent difference in behaviour.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text:
gradus/
  answers.scm      answer-file records, defaults, validation
  wizard.scm       page and field state machine (fields are plain data)
  render.scm       answers -＞ operating-system
  serialize.scm    answers and device map -＞ self-contained config.scm text
  storage.scm      partitioning, formatting, mounting, preservation rules
  install.scm      mount plan, guix system init, daemon lifecycle, logging
  utils.scm        subprocess handling, exit codes, secret files
  tui.scm          ncurses frontend (renders the wizard page model)
  script.scm       command-line entry point (--config / --answers / --tui)
tests/             SRFI-64 tests, one file per module

The layering contract — which module may import which, and the data contracts between core and frontends — is defined in docs/architecture.md. Modules live in the (gradus …) namespace. A module offered upstream moves to (gnu installer …) and follows the rules of that tree; a module in this repository never claims the (gnu …) namespace.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependency Use Guile 3.x Language runtime Guix Record types and the guix command guile-ncurses Terminal pages SRFI-64 Tests

No dependency is added to the installation image that Guix does not already carry, with the exception of the UI library.

docs.title: Coding conventions
docs.text:
The code follows the GNU Coding Standards and Guix's Coding Style, because part of it is intended to be offered upstream. The rules that actually change what a reviewer sees:

  • Pure functional style, except for input/output and low-level procedures.
  • Records, not lists. Use define-record-type* for data structures and (ice-9 match) for destructuring. Browsing lists with car/cdr is a review rejection.
  • Docstrings on every top-level procedure. Private procedures in a build-side module may omit them.
  • At most four positional parameters. More than that becomes keyword arguments.
  • Formatting follows Riastradh's Lisp Style Rules; the tree will carry a .dir-locals.el from the first code commit so that editors indent consistently. Indentation is not a matter of taste in a tree that takes patches by mail.
  • Module boundaries: build-side code in (guix build …) must not refer to other Guix or GNU modules; host-side code may use build-side modules.

docs.title: Language of prose
docs.text: The repository's own documentation and messages are in British English (see AGENTS.md). A patch written for Guix follows Guix's conventions, including its spelling and terminology. Do not "improve" an upstream patch to match this repository's voice; the patch belongs to the tree that will carry it.

docs.title: Upstream contributions
docs.text:
• Commit logs. Guix requires ChangeLog-format logs: a one-line subject such as gnu: foo: Fix bar., a blank line, then entries of the form * path/to/file (symbol): what changed. A body that only explains the motivation is not sufficient.
  • Sign-off. Every commit carries Signed-off-by: Name <email>, certifying the Developer Certificate of Origin. A patch without it is not merged.
  • Submission. Patches are produced with git format-patch --base and sent to guix-patches@gnu.org; each message becomes a Debbugs issue.
  • Checks. guix lint for package changes, make check for code, and ./pre-inst-env to run the tree's own commands. A patch that has not been built in the target tree has not been tested.
  • Licence. Guix is GPL-3.0-or-later. Code is not copied from this AGPL-3.0-or-later repository into an upstream patch: the patch is written for Guix and offered under Guix's licence. Confirm the current policy on guix-devel before sending anything non-trivial.

docs.title: Build and test
docs.text:
# In this repository
guix shell -D -f guix.scm -- make check

# Against a Guix checkout, for upstream work
./pre-inst-env guix system --help

A caution that cost a real debugging session: guix shell --pure strips the host PATH, so a driver that shells out to mount, losetup or partprobe will fail with execvp: No such file or directory. Run the installer either without --pure, or with the needed host directories restored explicitly.

guix.scm is added with the first code commit. Until then this document is the specification the code must satisfy.

docs.title: Installation flow
docs.text: The flow is modelled on two mature installers — YaST/Agama on openSUSE and Anaconda on AlmaLinux — because their stage boundaries have survived a decade of hardware and operator habits. What differs is the output: both of them leave a system, while Gradus leaves a system and the declaration that describes it.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
# Stage Agama (openSUSE) Anaconda (AlmaLinux) Gradus 0 Boot the medium GRUB entry, inst. options GRUB entry, inst. options GRUB entry, kernel command line 1 Language, keyboard, timezone separate dialogs Localisation hub Localisation page 2 Registration / product SUSE Customer Center Subscription (RHEL family) not applicable — channels instead 3 Installation source product repositories Installation source Source page: channels, substitutes, proxy 4 Network connections, proxy Network & hostname, proxy Network page: interface, host name, proxy 5 Storage partition proposal, manual Installation destination Storage page 6 Bootloader reduced set: menu stop, timeout, extra kernel parameters, NVRAM bootloader options: location, append, timeout, disabled Boot page 7 Software patterns and packages Environment groups, add-ons Software page: base profile, groups, names, manifest 8 Users root, first user Root password, user creation Users page 9 Review summary Installation summary hub Review page: full config.scm 10 Install progress progress Install page

Two structural notes:

  • Both reference installers use a hub (a summary screen whose sections can be visited in any order), not a strict wizard. The first release is linear because linearity is cheaper to get right; the pages are specified as independent so a hub can replace the order later without rewriting them.
  • Neither reference installer is declarative. Their "summary" is a summary of pending actions; ours is a file the operator can read, copy and install again.

docs.title: Bootloader
docs.text: The reference installers expose three things that matter on real hardware and that the official Guix installer does not ask about at all.

docs.title: Optional installation
docs.text:
Anaconda can be told not to install a bootloader at all (--location=none, also --disabled). This is not a curiosity: it is required when another bootloader owns the disk, when the machine is a virtual image, or when the operator will chain-load the system deliberately.

Gradus therefore treats "no bootloader" as a first-class value, not as an error. Choosing it:

  • leaves the existing bootloader untouched;
  • records the decision in config.scm (no bootloader field);
  • prints an explicit warning on the review page: the machine will not boot on its own until a bootloader is configured.

docs.title: Kernel parameters
docs.text:
Anaconda appends extra parameters (bootloader --append); Agama exposes extraKernelParams. This is how a headless machine gets console=ttyS0, how a workaround is applied before the first boot, and how an operator passes an installer-specific option without rebuilding the image.

In Guix terms these are kernel-arguments on the operating-system record. The page collects a list, shows the resulting line in full, and never hides parameters that a previous stage added.

docs.title: Menu policy
docs.text:
Setting Agama Anaconda Gradus Wait time timeout --timeout timeout Stop indefinitely stopOnBootMenu: true --timeout=-1 equivalent timeout: -1 Default entry — --default default-entry Update firmware NVRAM updateNvram --leavebootorder (inverse) update-nvram

A machine whose firmware entries are rewritten without being asked is a machine that may stop booting the operating system the operator wanted. The NVRAM option exists so that this is a decision, not a side effect.

docs.title: Kernel choice
docs.text: Guix has a decision the reference installers do not: which kernel package. linux-libre is the default; hardware that needs non-free firmware or drivers requires another kernel from an additional channel. The page offers the kernels available in the selected channels and states the consequence of each — a change of trust boundary, not merely of driver support.

docs.title: Network and proxy
docs.text:
An installation is a network operation long before the first package is unpacked: channels are fetched, substitutes are downloaded, and sometimes the answer file itself is fetched. On networks without direct egress, the operator needs a proxy at stage 3 or 4, before any of that.

The requirements, drawn from what the reference installers allow:

  • A proxy may be configured from the boot command line, so that a remote unattended installation can reach its answer file.
  • Both http_proxy and https_proxy are settable, and they may differ.
  • A no_proxy list is mandatory, not optional: a substitute cache on the local network usually must not go through the proxy that provides external access. Getting this wrong turns a fast LAN cache into a timeout.
  • The same values are applied to two places: the live environment (so the installation can fetch) and the target's Guix daemon (so the installed system can fetch). The daemon honours http_proxy and https_proxy in its environment, as documented in the Guix manual's Proxy Settings.
  • Whether the target's values are declared through the service configuration or through a wrapper around the daemon depends on the Guix release in use. v0.3 settles this against the supported release and proves it with test T6; until then the contract states the requirement, not the mechanism.

Credentials in a proxy URL are treated as a secret: they are written to the target only if the operator keeps them, and never printed on the review page beyond the host and port.

docs.title: Substitute services and third-party caches
docs.text:
The reference installers know about repositories; Guix knows about substitute servers, which are a different thing: a source of pre-built store items, verified by signature, addressed by hash.

The source page therefore accepts a list, not a single URL:

Kind Meaning Key required official The project's own build farms Already trusted mirror Another HTTP endpoint serving the official store paths, byte-identical and signed by the original builders No new key builder An independent builder, for example guix publish on the local network Yes — its own key

The distinction matters because it decides whether the operator must supply a key at all. A mirror that serves official artefacts needs no new trust; a local cache that builds its own artefacts does. Asking for a key for a mirror teaches the operator to click through key prompts, which is exactly the habit that makes signature checking worthless.

Ordering is significant: servers are tried in the order given, so the fastest reachable source goes first. A miss costs one lookup and falls through; a stale mirror cannot serve an old artefact, because the request is keyed by hash.

Every key accepted here is written into the target's guix-configuration as well as into the live environment. When authorize-key? is true — the default — the target's /etc/guix/acl cannot be edited later, so a key that is only authorised during installation disappears at the first boot.

docs.title: Assembled storage: RAID and LVM
docs.text:
The NAS mode assembles data volumes from disks that change over time. The design survives that because mount addressing is separated from assembly:

Layer What it is Identity assembly mdadm array, LVM volume group and logical volume member disks by disk-level identity (WWN, serial or GPT partition UUID), the array or volume by its own name and UUID file system ext4/btrfs on the assembled device the file-system UUID, unchanged when members are replaced declaration mapped-devices plus file-systems only the top two layers appear here

Consequences that the schema and the renderer must honour:

  • A replaced member disk changes the declaration's assembly section only. The mount section is untouched, because the file-system UUID inside the volume did not change.
  • Data volumes are adopted, never created implicitly: a data-volume entry carries the file-system UUID of the existing volume, and the installer assembles — but does not format — it.
  • Root and boot stay outside the data pool: gradus-root and GRADUS-ESP are independent of whatever happens to the data disks, which is why a failing data array cannot take the boot path down.
  • blkid reports the file system on an assembled device exactly as on a partition, so the label-to-UUID device map needs no special case.

Implementation-wise this means: the answer schema's storage section grows lvm and raid modes whose members are named by disk identity; the renderer gains a mapped-devices section translated from the assembly; and the prepare step assembles but never formats data volumes. None of it changes the mount-addressing rule decided above.

docs.title: What the review stage must show
docs.text:
Borrowed from both reference installers: a summary that is complete enough to catch a mistake before it is written to disk. Ours adds two lines they cannot show:

  1. The full config.scm, editable, with a diff against the profile it started from.
  2. The exact sources that will be used — channels, substitute servers, proxy — because those are the decisions that are hardest to notice after the fact.

docs.title: Page specification
docs.text:
The interactive installer is a sequence of pages over the generic configuration surface of a Guix System. This document defines what each page collects, what it defaults to, and which rule keeps it generic.

Rule 0: no page may mention a fleet, a role, a vendor or a site. Pages know about disks, interfaces, packages and bootloaders. If a page would need a proper noun that is not a standard system concept, it is a preset, not a page.

Rule 1: every page is skippable. If the value is supplied by --config or by an answer file, the page is not shown. Interactive mode is the union of pages whose values are still unknown.

Rule 2: the last page is always the configuration. There is no "apply" that the operator cannot inspect first.

docs.title: Page sequence
docs.text:
# Page Collects Defaults v0.1 1 Localisation language, territory, keyboard, timezone live environment's locale — 2 Source channels file, substitute services (name, URL, kind, key), proxy official channels, official substitutes, no proxy — 3 Storage disk, scheme (simple/LVM), encryption, swap, data volumes, erase consent no disk selected; erase off — 4 Boot bootloader (including none), target, kernel, extra kernel arguments, menu policy, NVRAM, generations kept GRUB EFI on the ESP, timeout 5 — 5 Software base profile, environment groups, extra packages, manifest file headless base — 6 Network host name, management interface, DHCP or static, wireless, proxy and no_proxy DHCP on the first wired interface — 7 Users root policy, user accounts, groups, SSH keys one administrative user, no root login — 8 Review full config.scm, diff against the starting profile, save to removable media — — 9 Install confirmation, progress, transcript — —

--config mode replaces pages 1–8 with a single validation step and goes straight to page 9.

docs.title: 1. Localisation
docs.text: Locale, timezone and keyboard layout. These affect the live environment and the target; they are written to the configuration, not only to the live session. Nothing here is inferred from the network: a wrong timezone is cheap to fix, but a silently guessed one is hard to notice.

docs.title: 2. Source
docs.text:
The page the official installer lacks. It collects:

  • a channels file (path or URL), defaulting to the distribution's own;
  • an ordered list of substitute services, each with a name, a URL, a kind (official, mirror or builder) and, for a builder, a signing key;
  • a proxy, with http, https and no_proxy values.

The same values must reach two places, and the page must show both:

  1. the live environment, so the installation itself can use substitutes;
  2. the target's guix-configuration, so the installed system keeps using them. When authorize-key? is true — the default — the target's /etc/guix/acl cannot be edited after the fact; the key must be in the declaration from the start.

One input, two destinations, never two lists.

The list is edited in place: add, remove, reorder. Order is visible because order is the policy — the fastest reachable source goes first. A "test this source" action fetches one narinfo through the configured proxy, so that a mistyped cache is discovered here and not twenty minutes into an installation.

The kind distinction is shown, not hidden: a mirror needs no key, a builder does. Presenting both as "substitute server" would teach the operator to accept key prompts without reading them.

docs.title: 3. Storage
docs.text:
Disk selection, partitioning scheme, encryption, swap and data volumes.

Non-negotiable behaviours:

  • A disk is written only after an explicit confirmation that names it.
  • A device already carrying a file system is shown as such and is not formatted unless erasure is requested for that device.
  • A data volume with erase? = #f is mounted, never prepared. This is how a reinstall preserves data.
  • Encryption is offered, never assumed.

The page produces file systems by UUID (not kernel device names), because the declaration outlives the enumeration order.

docs.title: 4. Boot
docs.text:
Bootloader family, target and policy, the kernel package, extra kernel arguments, menu behaviour and how many previous generations to keep.

Non-negotiable behaviours:

  • none is a value. Choosing it installs no bootloader and leaves the existing one untouched. The page states that the machine will not boot unaided; it does not refuse the choice.
  • Extra kernel arguments are listed, not concatenated silently. A headless machine needs console=ttyS0; a workaround may need one more parameter. The full resulting line is shown on the review page.
  • Menu behaviour is explicit: wait time, stop-at-menu (the equivalent of an indefinite wait), default entry, and whether the firmware's NVRAM is updated. Rewriting NVRAM without being asked can stop a machine booting the system the operator wanted.
  • The kernel package is chosen here. linux-libre is the default; another kernel from a selected channel changes the trust boundary, and the page says so rather than presenting it as a driver choice.

The official installer asks none of this, which is why a headless machine cannot be given a serial console at install time.

docs.title: 5. Software
docs.text:
A base profile plus environment groups plus free-form package names plus an optional manifest. It is deliberately not a catalogue browser: Guix has tens of thousands of packages, and a picker that pretends to rank them is worse than a text field with completion.

Selecting a base profile is choosing a starting configuration, not entering a code path. The resulting operating-system is shown on the review page, and a profile that cannot be expressed as a configuration is a bug in the profile.

docs.title: 6. Network
docs.text:
Host name, management interface, addressing, wireless credentials and proxy.

Static configuration is offered but not required; DHCP is the default on the first wired interface.

Proxy settings are collected here because everything after this page may need them: channels, substitutes, and a remote answer file. http_proxy and https_proxy may differ. The no_proxy list is a first-class field, not an advanced option — a local substitute cache normally must bypass the proxy that provides external access, and sending it through the proxy turns a fast cache into a timeout.

Wireless credentials and proxy credentials are the two secrets the installer must accept. Both are written to the target configuration only if the operator asks for them to be kept there; otherwise they are used for the live session and discarded.

docs.title: 7. Users
docs.text: One administrative account is created. Root login is disabled by default. Authorised SSH keys are collected as text or from a file; an empty list is allowed and leaves password authentication as the only route, which the page states plainly.

docs.title: 8. Review
docs.text:
The complete declaration, a diff against the profile it started from, and a "save to removable media" action. The operator may edit the text directly: the review page is the escape hatch for everything the other pages do not model.

Editing here does not bypass validation. The edited file is built before the installation starts.

docs.title: 9. Install
docs.text: A summary of what will be written where, one final confirmation, then progress with a transcript. The installer reports the step it is in, and on failure the state of the target as it actually is, not as it was intended to be.

docs.title: What is deliberately absent
docs.text:
• A package catalogue browser.
  • Service configuration pages beyond enable/disable and the fields a service exposes as ordinary values. Services are configured in the declaration; a general-purpose form generator over arbitrary Scheme records is a different project and a worse one.
  • Any page whose content depends on a site, a fleet or a vendor.

docs.title: Comparison with Anaconda and Agama
docs.text:
Checked against Anaconda's Installation Summary spokes (AlmaLinux/RHEL) and Agama/YaST (openSUSE Tumbleweed). What the two reference installers have that this page set must also have, or must refuse explicitly:

Concern Anaconda Agama/YaST Gradus Keyboard layout spoke yes missing — goes on the locale page NTP on/off with Time & Date implicit missing — goes on the locale page Timezone spoke yes yes Installation source media / network product + registration substitutes + channels (Guix is network-first; no local media) Software selection base environment + add-ons patterns base + free-form packages; profiles (planned) Partition sizes custom partitioning limited (a known Agama gap) must be explicit — ESP default 1 GiB is overridable, root is a size or the remainder LUKS encryption yes yes yes (LUKS1, root only — GRUB unlocks by UUID; LVM and swap combinations refused) Swap automatic yes an explicit size, defaulting to the machine's memory (1–8 GiB); refused with encryption Network interface choice, static addressing spoke yes DHCP only today; static + interface planned Root password / lock spoke yes yes User + "make administrator" spoke yes yes (wheel) KDUMP spoke yes refused — not part of a headless contract Security policy RHEL only no refused — vendor concept Bootloader page (menu, NVRAM update) implicit YaST yes timeout + kernel arguments; NVRAM update (planned) "Test this source" no no specified, not yet implemented

The two refusals follow from the contract: Gradus installs headless machines for this fleet, and a vendor security policy or a crash-dump daemon is a distribution decision, not an installer page.

docs.title: Acceptance tests
docs.text: A release is not a release until every test below passes on the release candidate. Tests are listed in the order they should be run: the cheap ones catch the embarrassing failures.

docs.title: T1 — Stranger test
docs.text:
Question: can someone who has never heard of this project install a normal desktop system with it?

T1 depends on the interactive pages and cannot be fully performed until the milestone that ships them. It is therefore staged:

  • T1-u (from v0.1): an operator who has read only this repository's README and docs/contract.md installs a system unattended from a configuration they wrote themselves, using --config, and finds the installed declaration where the contract says it is. No private identifiers anywhere in the output.
  • T1-i (from the pages milestone): the full stranger walk-through of the interactive installer, as described below.

Procedure (T1-i): a person who has not read the source boots the image, installs a desktop configuration with a wired network and one user, and logs in.

Pass criteria:

  • the installation completes without a shell;
  • the login session starts and the network works;
  • no page, message or artefact mentions a site, a fleet, a vendor or a proper noun outside standard system vocabulary.

This test is also a grep: the installer's user-facing strings and documentation must contain no private identifiers.

docs.title: T2 — Unattended test
docs.text:
Question: does an answer file produce exactly the system it declares?

Procedure: gradus --answers answers.scm --target DEV --erase, with no terminal attached.

Pass criteria:

  • exit status 0, no prompt, no hang;
  • /etc/config.scm is byte-identical to the file printed by --dry-run;
  • /etc/gradus/provenance.scm records installer version, contract version and Guix revision;
  • a second run with the same inputs produces the same declaration.

docs.title: T3 — Weaning test
docs.text:
Question: is the installer generic, or does it secretly depend on a particular configuration repository?

Procedure: install from a configuration written by hand for the test, with the preset directory removed from the image.

Pass criteria: installation succeeds. If it does not, the installer has grown a dependency on a preset and the dependency is the bug.

docs.title: T4 — Preservation test
docs.text:
Question: can a machine be reinstalled without destroying its data?

Procedure: install with a second disk carrying an existing file system declared as a data volume with erase? = #f; reinstall the system disk.

Pass criteria:

  • the data volume's contents are unchanged (compare checksums before and after);
  • the installer never writes to it;
  • a device carrying a file system is refused as a system disk unless --erase is given.

docs.title: T5 — Refusal test
docs.text:
Question: does it stop instead of guessing?

Cases that must fail with the documented exit status and a readable message:

Case Expected --target points at a mounted device 3 --target is the live medium 3 configuration references a label absent from the target 2 unknown key in the answer file 2 --erase without --target 1 UEFI bootloader declared, no ESP among the file systems 2

docs.title: T6 — Proxy test
docs.text:
Question: can an installation complete on a network with no direct egress, and does the installed system keep using the proxy?

Where it must run. In the Guix System live environment, not on a foreign distribution. Applying the proxy to substitutes means restarting the Guix daemon, and the installer does that through Shepherd (herd), which only exists on Guix System. A host running Guix on top of another distribution cannot exercise this path; the VM runbook in tests/vm/ is the place for it.

Status: not yet run end to end. The proxy environment itself reaches the Guix daemon in a live system; completing the installation inside the test VM is blocked by the rig, not by the installer.

Rig notes. Three things cost time and should be settled before a run:

  • A serial console backed by a file gives the guest's login shell EOF, so the shell exits and typed input lands on the login prompt. Use a pty and keep it open for the life of the VM.
  • The VM must hold a DHCP lease before hostfwd to port 22 can work; a refused connection usually means no address, not a missing sshd.
  • Before booting an image that is supposed to act on its own, confirm the service or special file is present in the built system — a declaration that builds is not proof that the activation ran.

Procedure: install with http_proxy/https_proxy set to a proxy that is the only route out, and with a no_proxy entry covering the local substitute cache. A logging CONNECT proxy is enough to prove the route: the installation must appear in its log.

Pass criteria:

  • channels and substitutes are fetched through the proxy;
  • the local cache is contacted directly (its access log shows the installation, the proxy's log does not);
  • after the first boot, guix build on the installed system still reaches the network without the operator exporting variables by hand;
  • proxy credentials do not appear in the transcript or in /etc/gradus/provenance.scm.

docs.title: T7 — Self-hosted cache test
docs.text:
Question: does a substitute service on the local network work during the installation and afterwards?

Procedure: run guix publish on a second machine; declare it as a builder with its signing key; install with external substitutes disabled.

Pass criteria:

  • the installation fetches store items from the cache (proof: the cache's access log, not the installer's claim);
  • the key is authorised in the live environment and present in the target's guix-configuration;
  • after the first boot, guix build uses the cache without further setup;
  • removing the key from the answer file makes the installation fail loudly rather than fall back to an unsigned source.

docs.title: T8 — No bootloader test
docs.text:
Question: is "do not install a bootloader" a real option rather than a refusal?

Procedure: install onto a disk that already carries a bootloader, with bootloader = none.

Pass criteria:

  • the installation completes;
  • the existing bootloader is byte-identical afterwards (compare the relevant partition or checksum);
  • the review stage warned that the machine will not boot unaided;
  • the resulting /etc/config.scm contains no bootloader field.

docs.title: Matrix
docs.text:
Every release candidate is installed at least once per row.

Axis Values Firmware BIOS, UEFI Bootloader installed, none Storage single disk, LVM, LUKS, separate /home Console graphical, serial (console=ttyS0) Network DHCP wired, static wired, wireless Egress direct, HTTP proxy, proxy with a no_proxy exception Substitutes official only, LAN mirror, LAN builder (guix publish) Memory 2 GiB (floor), 8 GiB Architecture x86_64 (v0.1+), aarch64, RISC-V (later)

Firmware and storage are the axes that break installers; they are never skipped for a release, even a documentation-only one.

docs.title: T9 — Encrypted root boots
docs.text:
Question: after an encrypted install, does the machine actually come up?

An encrypted root has two failure modes that no unit test can see: GRUB only learns the passphrase when the mapped device's source is a LUKS UUID (a device path is dropped with a warning), and the bootloader only speaks on the serial line when the terminals are configured. Either mistake produces a machine that installs perfectly and then does not start.

Procedure: install unattended with (encryption (mode . luks)) and swap-size 0 (a separate swap partition would sit in plaintext outside the container), then boot the disk with no installation medium attached.

Pass criteria:

  • GRUB asks for the passphrase on the configured console;
  • the kernel starts and the root is mounted from /dev/mapper/<name>;
  • the account created in the answers can log in;
  • /etc/gradus/provenance.scm names mode answers and the Guix that built it.

Last run (BIOS, LUKS1, serial console):

Enter passphrase for hd0,gpt2 (a0a35a9e-…):
NAME          FSTYPE      LABEL TYPE
└─vda2        crypto_LUKS       part
  └─cryptroot                   crypt
findmnt -no SOURCE /   →  /dev/mapper/cryptroot

Two rig notes, learned the hard way: a passphrase written to the console in one go is swallowed (type it a character at a time), and cryptsetup open --test-passphrase against the disk is the quickest way to separate "wrong passphrase" from "input not reaching GRUB".

docs.title: T10 — The console front-end installs, end to end
docs.text:
Claim: an operator who never opens a shell can install the system from the console front-end, and the installed system boots and accepts its login.

Procedure. The live medium is booted in a VM with the wizard on the virtual console; the walkthrough below was driven with virsh send-key (one keycode per call -- consecutive identical keys in a single call are coalesced by the guest, which silently corrupted names). Defaults were accepted everywhere except the account.

  1. Language page: Enter.
  2. Localisation, storage, software, boot, network: c accepts each form.
  3. Storage: the plan screen is accepted; the filesystem was ext4 (btrfs was verified separately, T9's medium had btrfs-progs).
  4. Users: name and passwords typed on the forms.
  5. Review: Enter on install; the log shows the four stages and ends with [4/4] installed; declaration kept at /mnt/target/etc/config.scm.

Evidence. After ejecting the medium the VM boots from disk to gradus login: (the host name comes from the answers), and root with the password entered in step 4 reaches root@gradus ~#.

Bugs this run caught (all fixed before it passed): a stray reviewed key rejected by the answer schema; a missing mkfs tool failing after partitioning; mount LABEL= racing udev; a duplicate getty fighting over ttyS0; the daemon ignoring the declared substitute URLs; and a comment swallowing a parenthesis that only the real front-end could reach.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
An installation counts as tested only when all of the following are attached to the release notes:

  • the installer transcript (/var/log/gradus-install.log);
  • the installed /etc/config.scm;
  • guix system describe output from the installed system;
  • for T4, checksums of the preserved volume before and after.

Screenshots are welcome but are not evidence: they cannot be diffed.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
The runbook for the virtual-machine procedure is tests/vm/README.md.

Virtual machines use QEMU with OVMF for UEFI and SeaBIOS for legacy boot, KVM enabled. At least one installation per release is performed on physical hardware, because firmware quirks and device enumeration are exactly what a VM does not reproduce.

Builds and VM runs are CPU- and I/O-heavy. They belong on a dedicated build host with KVM enabled, at least eight virtual CPUs and enough memory to hold two Guix System builds and a VM at once (16 GiB is a practical floor). Which host that is, in any given setup, is a matter for the operator's local notes; this tree does not name private machines.

docs.title: Product or upstream?
docs.text:
This project exists because Guix's installer does not cover the whole configuration surface. That is a gap in Guix, not a reason to build a parallel universe. The rule is therefore:

If a feature can be proposed to Guix as a self-contained patch, propose it. Keep here only what needs a product: the end-to-end flow, the unattended contract, and the disk-writing experience.

docs.title: Candidates for upstream
docs.text:
Feature Why it is generic Shape of the patch Substitute URL and signing-key page Every installation needs it; the current installer only toggles local discovery A page plus a field in the installer's configuration record Bootloader options page bootloader-configuration already models timeout, default entry, serial console A page over existing fields Configuration import (--config) Any operator with an existing declaration benefits Larger; requires an installer entry point that skips the wizard Package selection beyond desktop environments Every distribution's installer has it Needs agreement on where the package list comes from

The first two are small, self-contained and useful to everyone. They should be offered upstream before this project grows its own versions of them.

docs.title: Stays here
docs.text:
• The unattended answer-file contract (docs/contract.md). It is a product interface, not a Guix interface.
  • The storage flow, including the refusal rules and the preservation semantics.
  • Provenance artefacts on the target.
  • The release process, the VM matrix and the acceptance tests.

docs.title: Channels, and the nonguix question
docs.text:
A channel that ships non-free software (nonguix is the usual one) is a legitimate thing for an operator to choose and a thing the Guix project will never ship itself. This repository takes the middle position:

  • The installer is channel-agnostic, and that is all it does. Its source step accepts a list of channels — name, URL, commit — and nothing in the code knows what nonguix is. The same list is how a distribution mirror, a company channel or a personal channel is declared.
  • Concrete channels live with the machines they apply to. An operator's configuration repository is where a channel, its disclosure and its signing keys belong, because that is where the machines that use them are described.
  • Upstream patches carry the generic mechanism. That is the part that belongs to everyone.

An operator who wants a non-free channel has a supported, generic way to declare one without patching the installer.

docs.title: Rules for patches
docs.text:
1. No private identifiers. A patch containing a hostname, a domain, a private cache URL or a fleet convention is rejected before it is sent. Run the grep from T1 over the diff.
  2. No product-specific options. An upstream patch may not add a flag that exists only for this installer's flow.
  3. Behaviour first, page second. If upstream accepts the behaviour (for example, importing a signing key at install time), the page follows the accepted design rather than the reverse.
  4. Track what diverges. When a feature exists both upstream and here, record the divergence and the reason in the release notes. A silent fork becomes a compatibility trap.

docs.title: Cadence
docs.text: The installer targets the current Guix System stable release. Upstream changes to the installer's internals are expected; this project's own surface is deliberately thinner than a fork, so the rebase cost stays bounded.
